Zambia Restores Economic Activity as Border Dispute with Angola Ends

LUSAKA – Zambia’s economy sprang back to life this week after a three-week-long border dispute with neighboring Angola was formally resolved on Saturday, allowing trade and transport operations to resume nationwide.

The crisis began when armed skirmishes erupted in the remote Western Province border region, prompting authorities on both sides to close key crossings and suspend commercial transport. The closure of the Jimbe and Sikongo border posts brought cross-border trade to a near-standstill, disrupting the flow of copper exports, agricultural shipments, and imported fuel. Economists estimate Zambia lost $54 million in trade revenue during the standoff.

The government announced late Sunday that negotiations hosted in Lusaka, led by the Southern African Development Community (SADC), produced an agreement including joint border patrols and a commitment to review demarcation lines peacefully.

“Today, we are pleased to report that all crossings have reopened, and trucks are moving again,” said Home Affairs Minister Nchimunya Sitali. “Our priority was the safety of citizens and the restoration of normal economic activity.”

The Zambia National Chamber of Commerce welcomed the news. “Businesses across the country suffered severe delays and shortages,” said Chamber spokesperson Grace Mulenga. “It is vital for our economy that trade routes remain open.”

Transport companies like Copperway Logistics and Eastern Plains Freight confirmed that operations resumed Monday morning. Farmers in border regions also expressed relief, with maize shipments to Angolan markets picking up after weeks of uncertainty.

Analysts say the swift diplomatic resolution averted broader economic fallout, though some warn that underlying tensions must still be addressed.
